claims.text: 10 U.S.C. 119(g) verbatim: 'In this section, the term "defense committees" means-- (1) the Committee on Armed Services and the Committee on Appropriations, and the Defense Subcommittee of the Committee on Appropriations, of the Senate; and (2) the Committee on Armed Services and the Committee on Appropriations, and the Subcommittee on Defense of the Committee on Appropriations, of the House of Representatives.'

Amendment history from the GPO text: 2001 -- Pub. L. 107-107 substituted 'Subcommittee on Defense' for 'National Security Subcommittee' in (g)(2); 1999 -- Pub. L. 106-65 substituted 'Committee on Armed Services' for 'Committee on National Security'; 1996 -- Pub. L. 104-106 sec. 1502(a)(4) replaced the two original paragraphs, which had read 'the Committees on Armed Services and Appropriations of the Senate and House of Representatives' and 'the Defense Subcommittees of the Committees on Appropriations of the Senate and House of Representatives.'

Six committee/subcommittee units, each with a chairman and a ranking minority member, is the arithmetic behind the informal 'eight people' figure for a waived SAP -- but because the Appropriations Committee chair and the Defense Subcommittee chair are different individuals, the true ceiling under 119(e)(2) is twelve members, plus the staff directors added by DoD's own directive. Reasoning stated from 119(g) and DoDD 5205.07 (2010) para 4.f.

10 U.S.C. 119(g) defines 'defense committees' as the Armed Services and Appropriations Committees of the Senate and House plus the Defense Subcommittee of Senate Appropriations and the Subcommittee on Defense of House Appropriations - six bodies.

Public Law 107-107 (28 December 2001) substituted 'Subcommittee on Defense' for 'National Security Subcommittee' in 119(g)(2); Public Law 106-65 (1999) substituted 'Committee on Armed Services' for 'Committee on National Security'.
The House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform is not a defense committee within the meaning of 10 U.S.C. 119(g) and receives no report under that section.

desc: Section 119(g) defines the term that governs who gets told. As amended by Public Law 104-106 in 1996, Public Law 106-65 in 1999 and Public Law 107-107 in 2001, it means '(1) the Committee on Armed Services and the Committee on Appropriations, and the Defense Subcommittee of the Committee on Appropriations, of the Senate; and (2) the Committee on Armed Services and the Committee on Appropriations, and the Subcommittee on Defense of the Committee on Appropriations, of the House of Representatives.' The definition is the reason the SAP record is structurally invisible to the rest of Congress: the House Oversight Committee, which has held every public UAP hearing since 26 July 2023, is not a defense committee and has no statutory entitlement to the section 119 reports. Neither are the intelligence committees; they sit under a wholly separate regime in title 50. Before 1996 the definition was broader in one respect and narrower in another - the prior text referred simply to 'the Committees on Armed Services and Appropriations of the Senate and House' and 'the Defense Subcommittees of the Committees on Appropriations'. The 1996 amendment made the enumeration explicit. The practical consequence for this board: a member of Congress who is not on one of these six bodies and not on an intelligence committee has no lawful route to a SAP list at all, which is precisely the wall the 2023-2026 UAP oversight effort has repeatedly hit.
